title: How Cousteau and Gagnan built the Aqua-Lung in 1942–1943 and how scuba opened the sea to divers

facts.text: Before the Aqua-Lung, a diver holding his breath could reach about 60 feet and stay down for up to 80 seconds.
Helmet divers wore heavy rubberized suits, copper helmets and lead-soled shoes, and their air came down a hose from the surface, which limited how far they could move.
A 1925 device by Yves Le Prieur freed divers from the hose, but because its air flowed all the time, the supply ran out quickly.
Jacques-Yves Cousteau, a French naval officer, broke both arms in a car accident and took up swimming in the sea near Toulon to recover.
Cousteau's father-in-law put him in touch with Emile Gagnan, an engineer at France's largest gas company, Air Liquide, in Paris.
Because fuel was scarce during the German occupation of France, Gagnan had designed a valve that fed gas fuel to car engines.
Cousteau and Gagnan met in Paris in 1942 and adapted the valve into a demand regulator that releases air only when the diver breathes in.
The regulator supplies air at the same pressure as the water around the diver, which was a key safety feature.
In a first test in the Marne River east of Paris, Cousteau reached 30 feet; the device worked when he swam level but leaked air when he stood upright.
The inventors fixed the leak by placing the intake and exhaust tubes at the same level.
In 1943 Cousteau, Philippe Tailliez and Frederic Dumas made more than 500 dives with the device in the Mediterranean; by that autumn they had reached 130 feet.
The Aqua-Lung, invented in 1943, was first sold in France in 1946 and is part of nearly every modern scuba set.
Diving deep can cause nitrogen narcosis, a dreamlike state in which divers lose their quick reactions and their sense of danger.
In 1947 Maurice Fargues, a member of Cousteau's team, lost consciousness and died while trying to dive below 100 meters.
The Silent World (1956), a film Cousteau made with Louis Malle, won an Oscar.
Through his books, films and expeditions, Cousteau showed undersea life to a wide public and inspired generations of marine scientists and divers.
More than 28 million people have learned to scuba dive since the Aqua-Lung was invented.
Today volunteer scuba divers carry out visual surveys of fish and other sea animals in coastal waters, including national marine sanctuaries, and their records help manage these habitats.
NOAA estimates that more than 80 percent of the undersea world is still largely unknown.
